name: LORDY LORDY LOOK WHO'S ROQUEFORT-Y BURGER

recipe.history:
Roquefort is among the oldest and most storied cheeses on earth, its origin legend claiming that a young shepherd in the Combalou caves of southern France abandoned his lunch of bread and ewe's milk cheese to follow a beautiful girl and returned weeks later to find his cheese transformed by Penicillium roqueforti — the blue-green mold endemic to those limestone caverns — into something extraordinary. Whether or not the girl existed, the cheese did and does: Roquefort has been produced in the caves beneath the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in the Aveyron department of France since at least the eleventh century, when it was granted a royal monopoly by Charles VI in 1411. It is made exclusively from the raw milk of Lacaune ewes, hand-rubbed with mold, and aged in the natural caves where cold, wet air and native fungi do the slow work of transforming it into a complex, peppery, crumbly magnificence. In 1925 it became the first cheese in France to receive an Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, a designation that still governs every wheel produced today.

Blue cheese entered American burger culture tentatively in the 1980s and confidently by the 2000s, riding the same wave of European ingredient enthusiasm that brought truffle oil and arugula to mainstream restaurant menus. The "blue cheese burger" became a steakhouse standard precisely because the funky, salty, creamy intensity of mold-ripened cheese does something remarkable to beef — it amplifies the meat's umami while the salt content brings out sweetness you didn't know was there. Roquefort specifically — richer and more complex than domestic blues, with a lanolin-like quality from the ewe's milk that distinguishes it from cow's milk Gorgonzola or Stilton — elevates a burger from diner food to something that belongs on a bistro menu. Paired with a walnut butter and a honey-laced arugula, it transforms the hamburger into a vehicle for the entire tradition of French fromage culture.

I first ate Roquefort as a teenager at a dinner party hosted by my parents' friend, a Frenchwoman who set out a cheese board with the seriousness of someone arranging a religious tableau. She handed me a sliver of Roquefort on a plain cracker and watched my face as I ate it, and when I blinked — genuinely startled by how much it tasted — she smiled and said nothing. I have chased that experience ever since: the initial shock of the mold, then the butter of the sheep's milk, then the long, salt-and-pepper finish that sits on the back of the palate for minutes. I started putting it on burgers because I could not afford the cheese board and the bistro steak simultaneously, and I discovered that the beef did something to the cheese I had not anticipated — softened its aggression, filled in its acid with fat, made the whole thing rounder and more generous than either element alone.

A medium rare burger — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the only temperature at which you can place Roquefort on a patty and have the result make sense. The warmth of the beef softens the cheese just enough that it begins to melt at the edges without losing its structural crumble at the center, so that each bite has both the yielding creaminess of semi-melted blue and the sharp mineral pockets of intact mold veins. Cook that patty to well done and the cheese sits atop something dry and gray, unable to melt properly because there is no residual heat to coax it, and the whole combination turns into salt and bitterness without the fat to mediate. Medium rare is not sentimentality; it is the only chemical temperature at which these ingredients find each other.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
200g Roquefort cheese, crumbled into large pieces
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
1 medium shallot, thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Toast the walnuts: Spread walnuts in a dry skillet over medium heat and toast, stirring frequently, for 4–5 minutes until fragrant and slightly darkened. Cool completely, then chop finely.

2. Make the walnut butter: Beat room-temperature butter in a small bowl until smooth and fluffy. Fold in chopped toasted walnuts, fresh thyme, grated garlic, flaky sea salt, and cracked black pepper. Mix until evenly combined. Transfer to a sheet of plastic wrap, roll into a log, twist the ends to seal, and refrigerate until firm, at least 30 minutes.

3. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warmed milk and mix on low for 2 minutes. Knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, kneading until each addition is absorbed. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until the dough is smooth and elastic.

4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise for 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g each, shape into tight balls, and set on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and proof for 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

6. Make the honey-arugula: Whisk together honey, olive oil, and lemon juice in a medium bowl. Season with salt and pepper. Add arugula and toss to coat lightly. Do not dress until just before assembly so the greens stay crisp.

7. Form the beef patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions of 150g each. Handle as little as possible. Form each into a 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patty with a shallow thumb indent in the center. Season both sides generously with salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until it begins to smoke. Cook patties dry and undisturbed for 3 minutes to build a deep sear. Flip once. Immediately distribute crumbled Roquefort evenly over each patty — about 30–35g per patty. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes until the cheese begins to soften at the edges and the internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
9. While patties rest, slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a skillet with a thin film of butter over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.
10. Slice walnut butter into rounds about 5mm thick (one per bun half) and press onto the cut face of each warm toasted bun half so it melts slightly.

11. Assemble each burger: Place two slices of tomato and a few shallot rings on the walnut-buttered bottom bun. Set the rested Roquefort-topped patty on top. Dress the honey-arugula and pile a generous handful on top of the patty. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and press the top bun gently into place. Serve immediately while the Roquefort is still warm and softened.
